description: I’m Navraj, a 15 year old student developer from California who uses computer science to make invisible human crises visible and manageable. I’m drawn to the intersection of biomedical engineering and ethical software, which I plan to pursue in college, and I focus on building transparent tools that help vulnerable communities navigate physical and digital hardships. I’m a strong advocate for accessible technology, so I design mobile apps on everyday devices that are frugal and frontier.
summary:
DailyDil is health monitoring software that lets an astronaut check their own heart and circulation in about a minute a day, using only a camera that is already on board. A 30-second face scan and a 30-second palm scan read the small color changes each heartbeat makes in the skin, which is camera photoplethysmography, and return heart rate, heart rate variability, pulse-wave shape and beat regularity. Sleep, mood and temperature are typed in. Every indicator is shown against that astronaut's own in-flight baseline as green, amber or red, with one plain next step: scan again, drink water, confirm with the onboard cuff or ECG, or contact the flight medical officer.

NASA's Human Research Program lists cardiovascular adaptation as a risk of human spaceflight: fluid shifts toward the head within a day, blood volume falls, and blood-pressure regulation weakens. A Mars crew is roughly three years from a clinic, so the crew has to catch those changes itself.

We scan the palm as well as the face because palm skin carries far less melanin than facial skin, so the pulse signal holds up across skin tones, an equity gap already documented for pulse oximeters. No extra hardware, nothing to resupply, and all processing runs on the device, so the check still works during a communication gap.
details:
What it does:

Once a day, DailyDil app prompts the astronaut to run a check, as part of the mission routine. The face scan takes 30 seconds on the front camera, with an on-screen guide for distance and stillness. The palm scan takes 30 seconds with an open palm held in front of the same camera. The result screen shows six tiles: heart rate, heart rate variability, blood-pressure trend, rhythm regularity, sleep and mood. Each tile is colored against that astronaut's own rolling baseline rather than a population average, because a crew member's baseline itself moves in flight. Amber means scan again and follow one tip, such as drinking water or sleeping earlier. Red on two scans in a row means confirm with the onboard cuff or ECG and report to the flight medical officer. Tapping a tile explains what the indicator is, which spaceflight hazard it relates to, and when a reading is worth attention, so the tool teaches while it measures.

How it works:

Every video frame is checked for a face or a palm; the skin pixels inside that region are averaged to one value per frame; motion and lighting drift are filtered out; and what remains is the pulse waveform. The app scores signal quality and rejects a scan rather than return a number it cannot stand behind, and a rejected scan is simply repeated. Heart rate comes from the beat intervals, heart rate variability from their spread, rhythm regularity from how irregular those intervals are, and the blood-pressure trend from the shape of the pulse wave.

Why the palm, and why that matters for a crew. Published camera-pulse work is almost entirely face-based, and the face has two problems in space. Faces puff up as fluid shifts headward in microgravity, which changes the very region being measured. And camera pulse signals, like pulse oximetry, are weaker and more biased in darker skin, because melanin absorbs light before it reaches the blood: the bias documented in pulse oximeters is an optical problem, not a cuff problem, so a camera inherits it. Palmar skin is the least pigmented skin on the body and varies far less between people than the face does, which is why we made the palm the primary site and the face the second opinion. The palm is also large, hairless, well perfused and easy to hold steady, and a palm video carries none of the identity load of a face video. That choice is what we think is new here, and it is aimed squarely at keeping accuracy equal for every crew member on a mixed crew.

Tools:

The DailyDil app is Swift on iOS with the signal processing on-device; the models are quantized TensorFlow Lite, including a 1D convolutional network for heart rate. The project site is Next.js, React and TypeScript. The development dataset is 100 annotated videos recorded across skin tones and genders, evaluated with 10-fold cross validation. No server, no account and no network call is needed to finish a check, so nothing is lost during a blackout and no crew health data leaves the device.

What it does not do:

DailyDil screens, it does not diagnose. An amber or red result sends the astronaut to the cuff, the ECG or the flight surgeon; it never stands in for them. The blood-pressure trend and the rhythm flag are research-stage and are shown as trends, not as numbers to act on. A hospital validation study of palm camera photoplethysmography, with accuracy across Monk Skin Tone bands 4 to 10 as a pre-specified endpoint, has been designed with our mentor's research team, and DailyDil's own readings have not yet been tested against it.

Intended impact:

On a long mission this gives a crew a daily, equipment-free way to notice a change early, and gives flight medical officer a trend to read when a link is available. The same check runs on a phone on Earth for people who are far from a clinic for different reasons.
